prompt: An organization is enabling Claude Code for several teams. It needs to prevent unapproved model use and detect spend spikes before they affect the monthly budget. What should administrators establish before broad access?

options.text: Let users choose any model; review spending only after month end.
Verify model restrictions, spend controls, and alert response.
Force one cheap model and disable usage reporting for privacy.
Share credentials so all contributors appear as one identity.

feedback.reason: Model choice and spend are operational guardrails; set ownership and visibility before broad enablement rather than relying on post-month review.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The supported controls vary by product and organization setup; verify exact model, limit, and reporting capabilities before claiming enforcement.
details.scenarioApplication: Model choice and spend are operational guardrails; set ownership and visibility before broad enablement rather than relying on post-month review.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Usage visibility should avoid collecting unnecessary prompt content; the requirement here is spend telemetry and limits.
details.errorCorrection: Distinguish defaults, enforced limits, usage attribution, alerting, and the owner’s response.
details.transfer: Choose controls tied to budget and approved-use policy, then verify their effective operation.

messages.text: Month-end review is too late to act on the stated need for early spend-spike detection.
One cheap model does not establish task fit, and disabling reporting removes spend visibility.
Shared credentials obscure individual attribution and do not establish approved model use or alert handling.

prompt: A company’s fixed monthly cap is shared by five departments with very different expected request volume. A single global alert fires only after 95% of the cap is used. What should the rollout owner add?

options.text: Remove the fixed cap and leave all budget decisions to local teams.
Give every department the same low limit despite workload differences.
Allocate budgets; set earlier alerts and response owners.
Wait for exhaustion before assigning spending attribution or action.

feedback.reason: A late global alert lacks actionable ownership and may conceal one team’s spike; budget guardrails should match the organization’s usage model.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Cost attribution and limits need to be aligned with who owns budget decisions and how the system behaves at the limit.
details.scenarioApplication: A late global alert lacks actionable ownership and may conceal one team’s spike; budget guardrails should match the organization’s usage model.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A strict per-team cap can disrupt legitimate work; define escalation and exception processes.
details.errorCorrection: Distinguish defaults, enforced limits, usage attribution, alerting, and the owner’s response.
details.transfer: Make spend posture observable and actionable before rollout.

messages.text: Removing the cap abandons the fixed-budget constraint instead of improving attribution and response.
Equal low limits ignore the stated workload differences and may block legitimate work.
Waiting until exhaustion loses the chance for an actionable early response.

prompt: A team’s spend rises sharply after enabling an agent workflow that can make several calls per request. What should the admin compare before raising the team limit?

options.text: Compare only the model’s advertised unit token price.
Count enabled users and assume each task still needs one call.
Compare monthly bills without inspecting workflow changes.
Compare workflow calls, token usage, retries, and outcomes.

feedback.reason: Agentic interaction shape can multiply call and token usage, so a simple user count or unit price misses the drivers.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Spend growth may be acceptable if it buys valuable outcomes; compare cost against the workload and quality achieved.
details.scenarioApplication: Agentic interaction shape can multiply call and token usage, so a simple user count or unit price misses the drivers.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A limit increase should follow a measured explanation, not substitute for diagnosis.
details.errorCorrection: Distinguish defaults, enforced limits, usage attribution, alerting, and the owner’s response.
details.transfer: Connect usage signals to architecture and business value before changing guardrails.

messages.text: Unit price omits how many calls, tokens, and retries each workflow consumes.
The new workflow can make multiple calls; enabled-user count cannot represent that interaction shape.
An invoice comparison detects change but does not identify the workload or outcome drivers.

prompt: An organization’s API account has a monthly spend ceiling, but its rollout plan names no budget owner or alert recipient and defines no action near exhaustion. What is the main operating gap?

options.text: Assign the budget owner, alert recipients, and response.
Wait for a lower provider price instead of assigning budget duties.
Share one API key instead of defining budget response ownership.
Use prompt advice instead of an owned alert and response plan.

feedback.reason: A ceiling without ownership and response does not tell the organization who acts when the budget is near its limit.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Spend controls include who owns thresholds, who receives signals, and what the team does when they trigger.
details.scenarioApplication: A ceiling without ownership and response does not tell the organization who acts when the budget is near its limit.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Granularity depends on the organization’s product/account features; do not assume per-user controls unless verified.
details.errorCorrection: Distinguish defaults, enforced limits, usage attribution, alerting, and the owner’s response.
details.transfer: Make guardrails actionable and proportionate to actual usage ownership.

messages.text: A lower unit price does not assign the missing budget owner or alert recipient.
Shared authentication is not a budget response policy and can weaken attribution.
Prompt advice does not provide an owned alert or enforce the account limit.

prompt: A rollout has a €10,000 monthly budget. It sends an alert at €8,000, but that alert does not block requests. An exercise shows nobody receives or acts on it. What does the alert establish?

options.text: A hard cap that guarantees total spend cannot exceed €8,000.
A signal only; assign and test its recipient and response.
Automatic owner acceptance of all spend above the warning.
Proof that every in-flight request stops when the alert fires.

feedback.reason: A warning is a signal, not a hard spending limit or an executed response. Assign recipients and actions, test delivery and handling, and separately verify the actual limiting behavior.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A warning is a signal, not a hard spending limit or an executed response. Assign recipients and actions, test delivery and handling, and separately verify the actual limiting behavior.
details.scenarioApplication: A warning is a signal, not a hard spending limit or an executed response. Assign recipients and actions, test delivery and handling, and separately verify the actual limiting behavior.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Budget monitoring and enforcement have different semantics; verify both in the actual account and workload.
details.errorCorrection: Test the specific control and decision property required by the stated policy.
details.transfer: Connect measured usage and value to verified controls and accountable budget decisions.

messages.text: The stem explicitly says requests are not blocked at the alert threshold.
Configuration does not establish an authorized budget decision.
An alert does not stop in-flight work or prove enforcement.

prompt: An organization requires that only approved models be used. The rollout sets a low-cost default, but users can still select an unapproved model in a representative session. What is missing?

options.text: More reminders that the default model is preferred.
A higher default effort level for every task.
Enforce and verify the supported model restriction.
A shared user credential so selection looks consistent.

feedback.reason: A default selects the starting behavior; it does not enforce an allowlist. Configure the supported policy restriction and verify that the unapproved choice is actually unavailable or denied.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A default selects the starting behavior; it does not enforce an allowlist. Configure the supported policy restriction and verify that the unapproved choice is actually unavailable or denied.
details.scenarioApplication: A default selects the starting behavior; it does not enforce an allowlist. Configure the supported policy restriction and verify that the unapproved choice is actually unavailable or denied.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Use the product’s supported enforcement surface; do not assume every plan or deployment exposes identical controls.
details.errorCorrection: Test the specific control and decision property required by the stated policy.
details.transfer: Connect measured usage and value to verified controls and accountable budget decisions.

messages.text: Reminders do not enforce the stated approved-model boundary.
Effort changes work intensity, not which model the user is allowed to choose.
Sharing identity does not implement a model allowlist and weakens attribution.

prompt: A measured workflow improves correctly completed outcomes while using more calls per task. Cost, quality, and capacity trade-offs are documented. The authorized budget owner approves a higher ceiling with new alerts and response duties, and the controls are tested. What should rollout do?

options.text: Apply the approved budget revision and monitor the scoped workflow.
Reject all increases because any higher spend proves inefficiency.
Remove all limits because the owner accepted one increase.
Expand every unrelated workflow under the new ceiling automatically.

feedback.reason: The measured benefit and explicit owner decision support the scoped budget revision. Retain the approved limits, alert response, and outcome monitoring; additional expansion needs its own evidence.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The measured benefit and explicit owner decision support the scoped budget revision. Retain the approved limits, alert response, and outcome monitoring; additional expansion needs its own evidence.
details.scenarioApplication: The measured benefit and explicit owner decision support the scoped budget revision. Retain the approved limits, alert response, and outcome monitoring; additional expansion needs its own evidence.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Revisit the decision if workload, outcomes, or control behavior move beyond the approved assumptions.
details.errorCorrection: Test the specific control and decision property required by the stated policy.
details.transfer: Connect measured usage and value to verified controls and accountable budget decisions.

messages.text: Higher cost can be justified by valuable outcomes when the authorized owner accepts the measured trade-off.
Accepting a revised ceiling does not authorize unlimited spend.
Evidence for this workflow does not establish the value or readiness of unrelated workloads.
